## Sleep: Forgetting to Remember to Forget

by on July 16, 2009

in [Sleep Science](https://web.archive.org/web/20120628120817/http://blog.myzeo.com/category/sleep-science/ "View all posts in Sleep Science")

[![Starry Night](data:image/jpeg;base64, "Starry Night")](https://web.archive.org/web/20120628120817/http://www.flickr.com/photos/noahbulgaria/337797347/)It’s pretty well known now that sleep is important for [memory and learning](https://web.archive.org/web/20120628120817/http://www.myzeo.com/pages/76_memory.cfm), but if I told you that when you were about to fall asleep – you might not remember. In fact, remembering those times when you were awake or asleep over the course of the night is not as straightforward as it might seem.

## To Sleep, Perchance to Wake

A [recent study](https://web.archive.org/web/20120628120817/http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-2869.2008.00651.x/full) in the [_Journal of Sleep Research_](https://web.archive.org/web/20120628120817/http://www.wiley.com/bw/journal.asp?ref=0962-1105) by Feige etl al., has shown that people generally perceive their wake time with **just 45% accuracy**. Why?

Many people **think they’re awake when they were actually asleep**, especially if they have any sleep-induced [anxiety](https://web.archive.org/web/20120628120817/http://blog.myzeo.com/calming-a-racing-mind/) or sleep difficulties. Sometimes this can happen when you’re in REM sleep. Have you ever had one of those very realistic dreams in the morning when you think you’ve gotten out of bed, and then your alarm rings and wakes you up?

Other people may **think they’re asleep when they were actually awake**. It’s common to forget waking up in the middle of the night, especially if it was for a short period of time.  Studies (such as [this one](https://gwern.net/doc/zeo/2007-trajanovic.pdf "'Positive sleep state misperception – A new concept of sleep misperception', Trajanovic et al 2007")) have shown that short-term memories created within 3 minutes of falling asleep don’t transition to long-term memories very well.  [Another study](https://gwern.net/doc/zeo/1997-wyatt.pdf) has even shown that some people think they were asleep during periods of wakefulness that lasted more than 2 hours over the course of the night

On a different, but related note, **we often don’t remember our dreams**. Could this be associated with the difficulty to form long-term memories when we transition into and out of sleep? There’s no clear-cut answer from sleep science for that one just yet, but it’s a real possibility.

## What does this mean for the typical sleeper?

1.  The good news is that, whether you remember it or not, waking up from time to time during the night [happens to everyone](https://web.archive.org/web/20120628120817/http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CZ6W9Ipz7t0).
2.  Since short-term memories don’t translate well to long-term memories when you’re falling asleep, cramming up to the last moment isn’t going to help – [set aside some time to wind down](https://web.archive.org/web/20120628120817/http://blog.myzeo.com/prime-your-body-for-bed-the-power-down-hour%E2%84%A2/) into a good night’s rest.
3.  If you’re frustrated by the fact that you’re not remembering your [dreams](https://web.archive.org/web/20120628120817/http://www.myzeo.com/pages/62_dreams.cfm), there’s hope on this front – you can actually get better at remembering your dreams simply by writing them down in a dream diary right when you wake up each morning.

Do you find that you’re waking up more or less than you thought?  I know it certainly happens to me sometimes.  Share your experience in the comments or on [Zeo’s Facebook wall](https://web.archive.org/web/20120628120817/http://www.facebook.com/pages/Zeo/102892844923).
